messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 63

# Dr. Linh's Practice

Dr. Linh has been practicing dentistry for twenty-three years. Her small practice sits in a quiet strip mall, tucked between a dry cleaner and a tax preparation office. She arrives each morning at 7:15 to review patient charts and prepare the operatory, a ritual that has always steadied her. Her hygienists know her as meticulous, unflappable—the kind of dentist who notices a millimeter of recession on a molar and remembers every patient's fear of needles without being told twice.

Four years ago, a man began appearing in her waiting room. He would schedule appointments, then cancel. He would sit in his car in the parking lot. He left notes in her mailbox—not threatening exactly, but insistent. He knew details about her routine: when she arrived, when she left, that she always bought coffee from the café two blocks away on Thursdays. He knew her husband's name. He knew her daughter's school.

Dr. Linh reported him to the police. She obtained a restraining order. The stalking eventually stopped, but something in her didn't.

Now, three years later, she still arrives at 7:15, but not because she finds comfort in the ritual anymore. She arrives early because she needs to check the parking lot first—to walk the perimeter, to look under the cars, to make sure the building is empty. Some mornings, her hands shake as she unlocks the door. She tells herself it's just caffeine.

During patient appointments, she finds herself unable to fully concentrate. A man came in last week for a crown preparation, and she kept losing her train of thought. She couldn't remember if she'd already anesthetized the tooth. She had to excuse herself and check her notes. Her hygienist noticed. Everyone notices when you're not yourself.

The evenings are worse. Her husband, Marcus, will suggest they go out for dinner, and her chest tightens immediately. A restaurant means windows, means being visible, means not controlling who might walk through the door. She makes excuses. She stays home. She keeps the curtains drawn and checks the locks multiple times before bed—sometimes four or five times, even though she checked five minutes earlier.

At night, she dreams she's in the operatory with a patient, and when she looks up, the man is standing in the doorway. She wakes gasping, her heart throwing itself against her ribs. Marcus reaches for her in the darkness, but she flinches away. She doesn't mean to. She knows it's him. But her body doesn't believe it.

The worst part is the hypervigilance that follows her everywhere. In the grocery store, she positions herself so she can see the entrance. At the bank, she counts how many people are around her. Driving, she checks her mirrors constantly, convinced that the same car has been behind her for too long. She knows, logically, that he hasn't contacted her in three years. She knows the restraining order is still in place. She knows the police took it seriously.

But her nervous system doesn't know these things. It only knows that once, a stranger decided she was his, and that the world is not as safe as she believed it to be.

She continues to work. She prepares root canals and fits crowns and explains periodontal disease to anxious patients. She smiles. She is professional. But inside, she is always listening for the door to open, always bracing for something terrible that may never come.
